title: The Forgotten Socialist
author: John B. Judis
content:
![The Forgotten
Socialist](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/IMG_5376-1.jpg)

>  _American Socialist: The Life and Legacy of Eugene V. Debs_  
>  By Shawn Gude  
> Simon & Schuster, 416 pages, $30

Eugene V. Debs was the founder and four-time presidential candidate of the
American Socialist Party. In 1920, while in jail for opposing US entry into
World War I, Debs received almost a million votes for president. That
election, however, marked the last hurrah for Debs and the Socialists. The
Socialist Party crumbled and ceased to be a force within American politics.
Debs became, at best, a footnote in history textbooks. In 1978, Bernie
Sanders, out of work and politics, began a rough-hewn documentary on his hero
with the apt warning: "It is very probable, especially if you are a young
person, that you have not heard of Eugene Victor Debs."

But Debs's name is being heard again amid a [_revival of American
socialism_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-lefts-project-has-just-
begun/) for which Sanders can take considerable credit. The last biography of
Debs, by the outstanding labor historian Nick Salvatore, was
[_published_](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0252011481?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback&ref=compactmag.com)
forty years ago. This year, Simon & Schuster has brought out a 400-page
biography by _Jacobin_ contributor Shawn Gude, who has done his homework.

The book is noteworthy for highlighting Debs's support for racial equality and
for its portrayal of his prison years. Gude gives Debs his due for being an
early supporter of industrial unions and for putting socialism on the American
agenda before World War I, but he also recognizes Debs's failings as a party
leader and politician. He does justice to his subject's courage and conviction
as a public man without eliding his struggle with alcohol and his troubled
marriage. I have bones to pick with some of Gude's interpretations, but that
is to be expected when addressing the question of why Debs and the party
ultimately failed and what can be learned from these failures.
